tasks.locator: Methods › Setting; Results › Baseline Characteristics, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
tasks.source_read: Publisher full text (HTML), https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2833888, searched in the saved page text (scratchpad/vickers_page.txt)
tasks.extracted: At 14 community organizations that hand out strips in Kentucky, New York and Ohio (recruited May to December 2023), 414 of 732 analysed participants (56.6%) said they had used fentanyl test strips in the 30 days before the baseline survey; the authors call this higher than the median uptake of 19% in a scoping review and link it to recruitment at sites that hand out strips.

Before use, staff recorded a stated intention to reduce the dose after 142 of 391 fentanyl-positive checks (36.3%) against 7 of 122 negative checks (5.7%), crude OR 9.36 (95% CI 4.25–20.65), and an intention to dispose of the drug after 50 of 436 positive checks (11.5%) against 10 of 134 negative checks (7.5%), OR 1.60 (0.79–3.26). Intentions were stated to staff after the result and what people then did was not recorded; intentions were not reported for checks made after use. Editors' calculation (card): risk difference for dose reduction 30.6 percentage points (Newcombe 95% CI 23.3–36.3).

tasks.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, lower panel; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Before use, a stated intention to dispose of the drug followed 50 of 436 fentanyl-positive checks (11.5%) and 10 of 134 negative checks (7.5%), OR 1.60 (95% CI 0.79–3.26). The authors attribute the low rate to dependence on the drugs, lack of money to replace them and no access to unadulterated drugs, and contrast a 2015 festival service where 13% disposed of drugs after an unexpected result and 2% after an expected one. Editors' calculation (card): risk difference 4.0 percentage points (Newcombe 95% CI −2.3 to 8.7).

tasks.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 5th paragraph; Results › Outcomes related to models of DCS, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Disposal was observed in 5 studies and self-reported in 3, and was more frequent when results were unexpected: observed disposal at Canadian festivals ranged from 4% (n = 2078, 2015) to 7% (n = 2786, 2014); 10% of young adults in the United States disposed of the drug when fentanyl was detected (n = 81, 2017; the Rhode Island pilot); 0% of people who inject drugs did so in another US study (n = 125, 2017); in Canadian qualitative work (n = 20), people using opioids were less likely than people using stimulants to intend disposal if fentanyl was found. The review cites a UK festival (n = 230, 2016), the festival of Measham (2019), for clients' reasons for testing.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph; Strengths and Limitations, 2nd paragraph
tasks.source_read: Publisher full text (HTML), https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2833888, searched in the saved page text (scratchpad/vickers_page.txt)
tasks.extracted: The authors attribute the change from the crude to the adjusted estimate to people who used strips also doing things that raise overdose risk (using several drugs) and things that lower it (testing strength); they note that clients of harm-reduction sites are not representative, prior harm-reduction engagement was not measured, follow-up lasted four weeks, outcomes were self-reported, and anonymity prevented knowing why people were lost, including whether any died of overdose.

120 overdoses were recorded in association with checks, 113 of them among checks made after use; the authors caution that most checks were made after use and that the decision to check may have followed an overdose. The lower crude odds of overdose with a stated intention to reduce the dose (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.18–0.89) pool checks made before and after use, have no table and cannot be read as protection (card reporting issue); there was no comparison with visits without a check.

tasks.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 4th paragraph; Conclusions
tasks.extracted: Among 90 studies of drug checking services to October 2019, the only one linking intentions with health outcomes was the Vancouver supervised injection site study (lower odds of overdose, OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.18–0.89, among those intending to use less), repeated without the primary study's caveats; the authors call for research linking behaviour with health outcomes and for more rigorous designs.

tasks.extracted: Over four weeks, people who used strips at baseline had an adjusted composite risk-reduction score 0.86 points higher (95% CI 0.34–1.38) on a 0–15 scale, and reported more naloxone nearby (RR 1.10, 1.04–1.18), testing the strength of drugs before use (1.41, 1.24–1.61), asking someone to check on them (1.26, 1.10–1.45) and throwing out bad or unexpected drugs (1.50, 1.12–2.01), but less use by routes other than injection (0.86, 0.79–0.94); self-reported nonfatal overdose: adjusted RR 1.20 (0.70–2.06), unadjusted 2.06 (1.09–3.89).

Before use, staff recorded an intention to reduce the dose after 142 of 391 fentanyl-positive checks (36.3%) against 7 of 122 negative checks (5.7%), and an intention to dispose of the drug after 50 of 436 positive checks (11.5%); what people then did was not recorded.
